title: Measures and probability spaces
objectives: Build a probability space and prove continuity from above and below.

screens.title: Reaching +1
screens.prose: A fair walk starts at 0 and steps up or down by 1. Let $A_n$ be the event that it has reached $+1$ by step $n$. The chart draws 30 of 300 paths and counts the ones that hit the top.
screens.question: Fill in $P(A_n)$. Count the paths that reach +1 among the $2^n$ equally likely paths.

hints.text: List the paths of 3 steps and see which touch +1.
After 3 steps, 5 of 8 paths have touched +1. Four start with an up step, and the fifth goes down, up, up.
Of 16 paths of length 4, 10 have touched +1, so $\tfrac{10}{16} = \tfrac58$.

feedback.correct: $\tfrac12, \tfrac12, \tfrac58, \tfrac58$. A walk cannot first reach +1 on an even step.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the paths that touch +1 and divide by $2^n$.

byKey.r1c1: After 2 steps, the only new path is down then up, which is at 0. So the chance is still $\tfrac12$.
byKey.r2c1: After 3 steps, 5 of the 8 paths have touched +1: the 4 starting up, and down-up-up.
byKey.r3c1: A walk cannot first reach +1 on an even step. Four steps add no new path, so the chance is still $\tfrac58$.
byKey.r0c1: After 1 step, only up reaches +1: 1 path of 2.

explain.text: Reaching +1 for the first time takes an odd number of steps, so $P(A_2) = P(A_1)$ and $P(A_4) = P(A_3)$. Paths reaching it by step 3: UUU, UUD, UDU, UDD and DUU, which is 5 of 8. By step 4 there are 10 of 16, which is $\tfrac58$.

screens.title: The events grow
screens.prose: Slide through the steps. Each $A_n$ holds the paths that have reached +1 by step $n$, so $A_1 \subseteq A_2 \subseteq \cdots$. Their union is the event "the walk ever reaches +1".
screens.question: What does $P(A_n)$ tend to as $n \to \infty$?

widget.accept: 1: a fair walk reaches +1 sooner or later (recurrence)
widget.label: Limit

hints.text: The chance can only rise, because the events only grow.
At $n = 100$ the chance is 0.9204 and still rising.
A fair walk is recurrent: it reaches every level, so the limit is 1.

feedback.correct: 1. The union of the growing events is "ever reaches +1", and a fair walk does.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The chances rise with $n$. Ask what happens for every larger $n$.

byKey.read: You read the value at $n = 100$. The chance keeps rising for larger $n$.
byKey.half: That is $P(A_1)$. The chance rises as the events grow.

explain.text: The chances $\tfrac12, \tfrac12, \tfrac58, \dots, \tfrac{193}{256}, \dots, 0.9204$ rise towards 1. The fair walk is recurrent, so "ever reaches +1" has chance 1. We will prove that the chance of a growing union is the limit of the chances.

screens.title: Measures and probability spaces
screens.prose: A **measure** on $(\Omega, \mathcal{F})$ is a function $\mu : \mathcal{F} \to [0, \infty]$ with $\mu(\varnothing) = 0$ and countable additivity. $$\mu\Big(\bigcup_n A_n\Big) = \sum_n \mu(A_n) \text{ for disjoint } A_n \in \mathcal{F}.$$ A **probability measure** $P$ has $P(\Omega) = 1$. Then $(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, P)$ is a **probability space**.
screens.question: What turns a measure into a probability measure?

options.text: Every event has measure at most 1.
options.why: You used an upper bound on events. Half of length on $[0, 1]$ has all values at most $\tfrac12$ and is not a probability.
You named the property of every measure. Length on $\mathbb{R}$ has it and is not a probability.

options.text: The measure of every event is finite.
options.why: You used finiteness. Twice the length on $[0, 1]$ is finite and gives $\Omega$ measure 2.

hints.text: Look at the one number that differs between a measure and a probability.
Compare the total measure of $\Omega$.
A probability measure puts total mass 1 on $\Omega$.

feedback.correct: $P(\Omega) = 1$. The other properties hold for every measure.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what must hold for the whole space.

explain.text: A measure counts size: length, area, or a count. A probability measure is a measure of total size 1 on $\Omega$.

screens.title: Two tosses
screens.prose: Two fair tosses: $\Omega = \{HH, HT, TH, TT\}$, $\mathcal{F}$ is all 16 subsets, and each outcome has chance $\tfrac14$. The chance of an event adds over its outcomes.
screens.question: Fill in the chances of the three events.

hints.text: Count the outcomes in each event.
First toss H: HH and HT. At least one head: all but TT. HH or TT: two outcomes.
$\tfrac24$, $\tfrac34$ and $\tfrac24$.

feedback.correct: $\tfrac12$, $\tfrac34$ and $\tfrac12$. Each is a sum of $\tfrac14$ over its outcomes.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count outcomes and multiply by $\tfrac14$.

byKey.r1c1: At least one head is every outcome except $TT$: three outcomes.
byKey.r0c1: Heads on the first toss is $HH$ and $HT$: two outcomes.
byKey.r2c1: $HH$ and $TT$ are two of the four outcomes, so add $\tfrac14 + \tfrac14$.

explain.text: A probability on a finite space is a sum of outcome chances. Two outcomes give $\tfrac12$, three give $\tfrac34$.

screens.title: Length as a probability
screens.prose: On $[0, 1]$ the uniform pick of lesson 1 uses length: $P([a, b]) = b - a$. The two bars are disjoint, so their chances add.
screens.question: What is $P\big(X \in [0.1, 0.3] \cup [0.5, 0.9]\big)$?

hints.text: The bars do not overlap.
Add the two lengths.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the two lengths, and skip the gap between them.

byKey.span: You measured from 0.1 to 0.9, gap included. The gap from 0.3 to 0.5 is not in the event.
byKey.one: You counted the whole space. Only the two bars are in the event.

explain.text: The bars are disjoint, so $P$ adds: $0.2 + 0.4 = 0.6$. The gap of length 0.2 and the end pieces hold the other 0.4.

screens.title: Continuity from below
screens.prose: Let $A_1 \subseteq A_2 \subseteq \cdots$ and $A = \bigcup_n A_n$. We prove $P(A_n) \to P(A)$. Two lines are flawed.
screens.question: Put the proof in order, a reason in each line. Move the two flawed lines to Left out.

lines.text: Set $B_1 = A_1$ and $B_n = A_n \setminus A_{n-1}$. The $B_n$ are disjoint, because the $A_n$ increase.
$\bigcup_n B_n = A$, because each point joins at the first $A_n$ that holds it.
That sum is $\lim_n \sum_{k \le n} P(B_k)$, by the definition of a series. Each partial sum equals $P(A_n)$, by finite additivity, since $A_n = B_1 \cup \cdots \cup B_n$.

lines.why: You added the $A_n$ themselves. They overlap, so the early sets are counted many times.
You gave an example of a limit. The proof must hold for every increasing sequence.

hints.text: Cut the union into disjoint pieces, then add.
Countable additivity needs disjoint sets, so build the $B_n$ before it is used.
Order: define $B_n$, their union, additivity, series limit with partial sums, conclusion.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Define the disjoint pieces before you add chances.

byKey.d1: You used the line that adds the $A_n$. The $B_n$ are the disjoint pieces.
byKey.d2: You used an example, not a step.
byKey.left-out: You left out a line the proof needs. Only the two flawed lines go to Left out.

explain.text: Cutting each $A_n$ into new slices $B_n$ makes disjoint sets, so countable additivity applies. The partial sums of the slices rebuild $P(A_n)$, and their limit is $P(A)$. This is continuity from below.

screens.title: Continuity from above
screens.prose: Now let $A_1 \supseteq A_2 \supseteq \cdots$ with $A = \bigcap_n A_n$ and $P(A_1) < \infty$. Then $A_1 \setminus A_n$ increases to $A_1 \setminus A$, so $P(A_1 \setminus A_n) \to P(A_1 \setminus A)$ by the last proof. The bars show $A_n = (0, \tfrac1n]$.
screens.question: Which step needs $P(A_1) < \infty$?

options.text: Writing $P(A_1 \setminus A_n) = P(A_1) - P(A_n)$ and then cancelling $P(A_1)$.
Saying $A_1 \setminus A_n$ increases as $n$ grows, since $A_n$ shrinks.
options.why: You blamed the increasing step. It holds because $A_n$ shrinks, whatever the sizes.

options.text: Applying continuity from below to the sets $A_1 \setminus A_n$ in turn.
options.why: You blamed continuity from below. It holds for any measure.

options.text: Writing $A$ as the intersection of all the sets $A_n$ at once.
options.why: You blamed the definition of $A$. An intersection exists whatever the sizes.

hints.text: Subtraction of two chances is the suspicious step.
$\infty - \infty$ is undefined.
If $P(A_1) = \infty$, then $P(A_1) - P(A_n)$ means nothing.

feedback.correct: The subtraction. With $P(A_1)$ finite, $P(A_n) \to P(A)$ follows.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look for the step that subtracts one measure from another.

byKey.b: The sets increase because the $A_n$ decrease.
byKey.c: Continuity from below needs no finiteness.
byKey.d: Intersections do not need it either.

explain.text: $P(A_1 \setminus A_n) = P(A_1) - P(A_n)$ makes sense only when $P(A_1)$ is finite. Then $P(A_1) - P(A_n) \to P(A_1) - P(A)$, so $P(A_n) \to P(A)$. For the bars, $P(A_n) = \tfrac1n \to 0 = P(\varnothing)$.

screens.title: The union bound
screens.prose: Three desks each breach a risk limit on a given day with chance 1%. We know nothing about how the breaches relate. The union bound says $P\big(\bigcup_k A_k\big) \le \sum_k P(A_k)$.
screens.question: What is the most the chance of at least one breach can be?

widget.accept: 3%: the bound, reached when the breaches never overlap
widget.label: Largest chance

hints.text: Overlaps can only make the union smaller.
The union is at most the sum, and the sum is $1 + 1 + 1$.
If the breaches never overlap the union equals the sum, so 3% is reached.

feedback.correct: 3%. The union bound holds for any dependence, and disjoint breaches reach it.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the three chances.

byKey.indep: You assumed independent desks, which gives 2.9701%. Disjoint breaches give more, so independence is not the largest.

explain.text: Take the pieces $B_k = A_k \setminus (A_1 \cup \dots \cup A_{k-1})$. They are disjoint, each lies inside $A_k$, and they have the same union. So $P(\bigcup A_k) = \sum P(B_k) \le \sum P(A_k)$.

screens.title: Continuity from above, with infinite length
screens.prose: Length on $\mathbb{R}$ is a measure. Let $A_n = [n, \infty)$. The sets decrease, and $\bigcap_n A_n = \varnothing$, which has length 0. A colleague applies continuity from above.
screens.question: What is $\lim_n \text{length}(A_n)$?

options.text: $\infty$, since every $A_n$ has infinite length, so continuity from above fails.
0, by continuity from above, since the intersection of the sets is empty.
options.why: You applied continuity from above. It needs $P(A_1) < \infty$, and here every $A_n$ has infinite length.

options.text: 1, since each set is one unit shorter than the one before it, so one remains.
options.why: You counted units removed. Removing a finite piece from an infinite set leaves infinite length.

options.text: It does not exist, because the lengths never settle to one value.
options.why: You said the limit fails to exist. It exists: every term is $\infty$.

hints.text: What is the length of each $A_n$?
Every $A_n$ is a ray that never ends.
The limit of $\infty, \infty, \dots$ is $\infty$, and the length of $\varnothing$ is 0.

feedback.correct: $\infty$. Continuity from above fails here because $P(A_1)$ is not finite.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the finiteness condition before you use the theorem.

byKey.c: Infinite length minus any finite piece is still infinite.
byKey.d: A constant sequence has a limit.

explain.text: Each $A_n$ is a ray of infinite length, so the limit is $\infty$. The intersection is empty, with length 0, so the two sides differ. On a probability space $P(A_1) \le 1$, so the condition always holds there.

screens.title: The exact chance in code
screens.prose: Write `hit_prob(n)`, the exact chance a fair walk has reached $+1$ within $n$ steps, as a `Fraction`. Do not list all $2^n$ paths. Track the chance of each position not yet at +1. Each step, add the chance that reaches +1 to a running total.
screens.question: Complete `hit_prob`.

widget.starter:
from fractions import Fraction

def hit_prob(n):
    """Exact chance a fair +-1 walk from 0 has reached +1 within n steps."""
    ...

tests.call: all(hit_prob(n) <= hit_prob(n + 1) for n in range(0, 25))

widget.how: Check runs 9 hidden tests with exact fractions. They include n = 100, which a path listing cannot reach, and a check that the chances never fall.

hints.text: Keep a dictionary from position to chance, for walks that have not yet touched +1.
Each step splits every chance in half, up and down. A step to +1 adds to `hit` and leaves the dictionary.
The positions run from `-n` to 0, so the work grows like $n^2$.

feedback.correct: Right. The exact chance of a path-by-path count agrees, and $n = 100$ gives $1 - \binom{100}{50}/2^{100} \approx 0.9204$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Return a `Fraction`, and drop a walk once it touches +1.

explain.text: The dictionary holds the chance of each position among walks that have not touched +1. Each step halves and moves it, and the chance that reaches +1 joins `hit`. It is the growing events $A_n$, one step at a time.

screens.title: Default sooner or later
screens.prose: A credit desk assumes a constant 2% chance of default each year, with independent years. Let $A_n$ be "default by year $n$". Then $P(A_n) = 1 - 0.98^n$, and the events grow with $n$.
screens.question: Fill in the chances, then the chance of "default some time".

hints.text: Use $1 - 0.98^n$ for the first two.
The union of the growing events is "default some time", and its chance is the limit of $1 - 0.98^n$.
$0.98^n \to 0$, so the limit is 1. Continuity from below gives the chance of the union.

feedback.correct: 0.1829, 0.6358 and 1. Continuity from below turns the limit of the chances into the chance of the union.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. $P(A_n) = 1 - 0.98^n$, and the last row is its limit.

explain.text: $1 - 0.98^{10} = 0.1829$ and $1 - 0.98^{50} = 0.6358$. The events $A_n$ grow, and $P(A_n) \to 1$. Continuity from below says the union, "default some time", has chance exactly 1.

ideas: A measure is a countably additive size on a sigma-algebra. A probability space $(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, P)$ has $P(\Omega) = 1$.
Increasing events: $P(A_n) \uparrow P(\bigcup A_n)$. Decreasing events with finite $P(A_1)$: $P(A_n) \downarrow P(\bigcap A_n)$.
The union bound caps a union by the sum of chances. An event of chance 1 holds almost surely.

formula.name: Continuity from below
formula.note: Slice into disjoint pieces and add.

summary.trap: Continuity from above needs a finite starting measure: $[n, \infty)$ shrinks to $\varnothing$ but keeps infinite length.

quiz.prose: The uniform pick $X$ on $[0, 1]$ is irrational with chance 1, yet some picks are rational.
quiz.question: What do we call an event of chance 1 that is not $\Omega$, such as "$X$ is irrational"?

options.why: You said sure. A sure event is $\Omega$, and the rationals are in $\Omega$ but not in the event.
You said impossible. The event has chance 1, so its complement has chance 0.

feedback.correct: Almost sure: it fails only on a set of chance 0.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Chance 1 is not the same as containing every outcome.

explain.text: An event of chance 1 holds "almost surely". The exceptions, the rationals, form a set of chance 0.

quiz.prose: Four desks each breach a limit with chance 0.5%, with unknown dependence.
quiz.question: What is the smallest bound the union bound gives for at least one breach?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the four chances.

byKey.indep: You assumed independent desks, which gives 1.985%. The union bound holds for any dependence, so it is 2%.

explain.text: The union bound adds the chances: $4 \times 0.5\% = 2\%$. Independent desks give $1 - 0.995^4 = 1.9850\%$, just under it.

quiz.prose: Under the uniform pick, let $A_n = (0, \tfrac1n]$, so $P(A_n) = \tfrac1n$.
quiz.question: What is $P\big(\bigcap_n A_n\big)$?

feedback.correct: 0: continuity from above, since $P(A_1) = 1$ is finite.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The sets shrink to the empty set.

byKey.one: You gave $P(A_1)$. The sets shrink to the empty set, whose chance is 0.

explain.text: No positive number lies in every $(0, \tfrac1n]$, so the intersection is empty. Continuity from above agrees: $P(A_n) = \tfrac1n \to 0$.

quiz.prose: A constant 2% default chance each year, independent.
quiz.question: What is the chance of default by year 20?

byKey.lin: You added 2% twenty times. That counts overlaps, so it is the union bound, not the chance.
byKey.one: That is the chance of no default, $0.98^{20}$. Take it from 1.

explain.text: $0.98^{20} = 0.6676$, so the chance of default by year 20 is $1 - 0.6676 = 0.3324$. Adding 2% twenty times gives 0.4, which counts overlaps.
